schools.summary: Matthew Henry reads the challenge as the application of the whole survey of nature: God pauses, then, though Job is silent, answers his very silence, perhaps in a still small voice as to Elijah.
Gill takes the pause the same way — God stopped that Job might answer, and finding him silent, began again.
Clarke argues 'answered' refers to nothing Job said, and that vv.1-14 are really the poem's displaced ending, belonging after Job 42:6.

debates.question: Do the opening verses of Job 40 stand in their original place?

sides.position: they are dislocated and belong after Job 42:6, so Jehovah is the poem's last speaker
the verses stand in their received place, opening God's second address

schools.summary: Keil reads the question as a climax — Job not only contended with God but doubted the divine justice; Ellicott renders 'Can the contending instruct him?' and sets it in God's argument from the beasts.
Gill presses the absurdity — he who disputes with the God of knowledge ought to be able to instruct him, which is folly.
Clarke: let the man who has made so free with God answer to what he has heard.

outliers.note: Allows that Job's resolve in vv.4-5 might be transposed after Job 42:6 as the poem's climax, but judges it neither necessary nor supported by any external evidence.

schools.summary: Keil marks the shift of address — Job answers Jehovah, not his friends — and reads it as the point where the divine speech has attained its end, effecting free submission, not blind subjection.
Gill catches the reluctance: finding himself obliged, Job answered, but with some reluctance.

themes: the shift of address to Jehovah
the divine speech attaining its end

schools.summary: Henry traces the descent of the penitent: Job comes to himself, owns himself an offender, and lays his hand on his mouth, for repentance changes men's opinion of themselves.
Gill turns 'vile' over in several senses — light words, works found wanting, original meanness, or the sinfulness of his nature now laid bare.
Clarke keeps it bare and personal: 'I acknowledge my inward defilement... I must be dumb before thee.'
Keil reads 'once, yea twice' as the idiom for what was done repeatedly, and hears true submission — Job lays down the cause, God speaking not in wrath but in condescension.
Clarke: 'I shall attempt to justify myself no longer... all is impurity in the presence of thy Majesty' — though he still refers the resolve to the poem's true climax after Job 42:6.
Gill takes the words as a settled resolve to answer no more, noting Jarchi's view that Job retracts earlier words.

themes: the hands of God versus the hands of men

schools.summary: Henry makes the renewed speech a law of the spiritual life: those who profit hear more, and the penitent must not catch at comfort too soon but let the wound be searched to the bottom.
Gill judges the whirlwind continued and increased, God requiring a fuller confession than that Job was merely vile.
Keil hears the storm as mercy — God speaks again to persuade, not to crush, bringing his servant to free and glad knowledge.

themes: the second speech from the whirlwind
not catching at comfort too soon
searching the wound to the bottom

schools.summary: Keil reads 'gird up thy loins' as the summons of a combatant, the challenge rising to a climax: can Job, who would govern better, show an arm and thunder as God does?
Gill notes the bare demand — Job to gird himself like a man, God to ask and he to answer.
Clarke refers the summons back to Job 38:3 and takes the repeated words as a seam where displaced leaves of the roll were stitched together.

themes: "gird up thy loins like a man"

schools.summary: Keil renders 'Wilt thou annul my right?' and reads the speech as testing Job to put on the King's robes; Ellicott unfolds the argument from the beasts to the government of men.
Gill takes 'my judgment' as God's decrees and sentence, which cannot be disannulled, his judgment being according to truth.
Clarke exposes the deeper fault: rather than be thought wrong, Job would condemn God — the three hardest words being 'I am wrong.'

themes: governing the world and treading the wicked

schools.summary: Henry draws out the two things denied Job — he can neither fight it out (his forces but briers before a fire) nor talk it out, God's thunder drowning his whispers.
Gill: God's power is infinite and uncontrollable — the arm that upholds the saints can crush his enemies like a moth.
Clarke feels the cumulative force: every word here tends to humble the soul, till Job fell in the dust confounded.
Keil keeps the clauses interrogative: in ruling the world God shows his arm and thunders — can Job do the like?
Henry unfolds the comparison: let Job robe himself in all his pomp, it is but a glow-worm to the sun, for God's majesty is the terror of devils and the wonder of angels.
Keil reads a mock-investiture — Job to put on the robes of the King of kings and send forth wrath, that the offer show him the gulf he cannot cross.
Gill: deck thyself with such majesty as God is clothed withal, a garment no creature can counterfeit.
Clarke turns it on Job's presumption: act like God, since thou hast assumed his perfections.
Henry makes the verse a proof of Godhead: God proves himself God in resisting the proud, who go before destruction and are brought low with a look.
Keil renders 'the overflowings of thy wrath,' recalling the prophets' judgment on pride, which God alone can pour where it belongs.
Gill: work thyself into a king's passion and try whether thy menaces can humble a proud man — as Job's rage toward heaven could not.

themes: God proved God by resisting the proud

schools.summary: Henry: if Job can abase the proud as God can, he has some colour to compete; but he murmured at oppressors' prosperity, and ought not to find fault except he could mend.
Keil carries the sense from the flood of wrath: Job to cast down the evil-doers in their place, a dominion reaching every proud man in his stronghold.
Gill dwells on 'in their place' — the wicked trodden down wherever found, their pretended rootedness no security.

themes: treading the wicked in their place

schools.summary: Henry follows the judgment to the grave: the proud not merely brought to the dust but hidden in it, like the Egyptian Moses hid in the sand, bound and buried in oblivion.
Gill reads the hiding as an inglorious burial in a common pit, the word also rendered 'alike' — high and low levelled in one ruin.
Clarke takes 'bind their faces in secret' of the custom of mummy-wrapping, every feature swathed out of sight.

outliers.note: Reads 'bind their faces in secret' literally of embalming — the mummy's head rolled about with filleting so that not a feature shows, the real face bound out of sight for ever.

themes: hiding the proud in the dust

schools.summary: Clarke makes the verse the crown of the speech: only when Job can wield God's arm and glory will God own that his right hand can save him — meaning salvation belongs to the LORD, and without Jesus every spirit must perish.
Henry hears a rebuke of man's oldest ambition to be his own saviour; our hands cannot save by winning grace or escaping justice, so into God's hand we must commit ourselves.
Gill spells out the impossible concession: since Job can do none of these, his own hand cannot save him, and only the arm of the LORD works salvation.

themes: "thine own right hand can save thee"
man's ambition to be his own saviour

schools.summary: Gill notes the plural name, commonly taken of the elephant, but reports Bochart's dissent for the hippopotamus.
Henry sees no reason to leave the ancient received opinion that it is the elephant, setting aside bull and river horse.
Clarke breaks with both, holding with Mr. Good that the creature is extinct — the mammoth, whose bones argue a beast twenty-five feet high.
Ellicott finds the identification a standing difficulty, the plural name perhaps covering two animals (elephant then hippopotamus), and notes a Coptic 'water-ox' concealed in the word.
Gregory the Great reads Behemoth allegorically as the ancient enemy, whose hunger the proud feed with their teeming thoughts as with the hay of the field.

sides.position: the elephant — the ancient and generally received opinion
perhaps two animals — elephant in the earlier verses, hippopotamus in the later
not a beast at all, but the ancient enemy read allegorically

outliers.note: Alone reads the passage allegorically, taking Behemoth for the devil rather than any brute — the proud grow the more devoted to him as they swell with worldly success.

schools.summary: Keil reads the strength in the loins and belly-sinews as the frame of the giant of beasts; Ellicott corrects 'navel' to 'sinews,' lodging the force in the great cords of the body.
Gill grants the elephant's known strength, but adds candidly that 'what follows does not seem so well to agree' with it.
Clarke refers the loins to agility — the vast springs and bounds of his leaping mammoth.
Gill argues the tail is compared to a cedar not for length but for firmness and thickness, like the river horse's, and gathers a crowd of older renderings.
Clarke makes the cedar-tail a proof against both elephant and hippopotamus, pointing to a leaping animal, and reads the second clause of the sinews of the haunches.
Ellicott corrects the 'sinews of his stones' to the sinews of his thighs.

debates.question: Does the tail 'like a cedar' fit the elephant or hippopotamus?

sides.position: neither — a leaping animal, the mammoth
the river horse, whose tail is firm and twisting

outliers.note: Reports Junius and the Targum referring the word not to the tail at all but to another extreme part of the body, Cicero noting the ancients so named it.

schools.summary: Gill hears the doubled figure as emphasis, but objects that brass-and-iron bones ill fit the elephant, whose bones are porous and spongy; the river horse's teeth are harder than ivory.
Clarke reads the iron bones toward his mammoth, the tusk uncommonly hard and weighty.
Ellicott renders 'strong pieces' as perhaps tubes — the limbs like bars of iron.

outliers.note: Argues the 'bones as brass and iron' tell against the elephant, whose bones the anatomists show to be porous and spongy save the ivory teeth.

schools.summary: Henry hears in 'his Maker can make his sword approach' the great use of the whole: God can unmake the beast at pleasure, and Behemoth images the proud tyrants he had bidden Job abase.
Ellicott judges 'chief of the ways of God' fitter for the elephant's intelligence, and lays out the obscure sword-clause in its rival renderings.
Gill reads 'chief' as the first-made (of the fifth day) or the head of its kind — the river horse, chief of the amphibious animals.
Clarke seizes the title for the mammoth, the largest, strongest, and swiftest quadruped God has formed.

debates.question: Which creature is 'the chief of the ways of God'?

sides.position: the elephant, for its intelligence and usefulness
the river horse, chief of the amphibious animals (or first-made, of the fifth day)
the mammoth, largest, strongest, and swiftest quadruped

themes: Behemoth as image of proud tyrants

schools.summary: Keil turns to the botany — the shade-tree is the lote (Rhamnus), found by the Sea of Galilee — and reads the grazing beast as harmless, the field-beasts playing beside it.
Gill makes the mountain-grass an argument for the amphibious river horse that leaves the water to feed, citing the northern morss that climbs to the heights.
Clarke takes the mountains as decisive against the water-bound hippopotamus and for the land-ranging mammoth.

debates.question: Do the mountain pastures suit the river horse or rule it out?

sides.position: against the water-bound hippopotamus, for the land-ranging mammoth
the river horse, which leaves the water to graze the heights

outliers.note: Offers the northern morss (walrus/sea-horse), which climbs by its great teeth to the mountain-tops to feed and rolls back into the sea, as a parallel for the amphibious behemoth.

themes: the beasts of the field at play

schools.summary: Henry sets the beast's shady lodging against the lion's dark den: those who let others be easy have nothing to fear, the reeds and willows enough for a creature that designs no harm.
Ellicott thinks the resting-place fitter for the elephant, and exposes the biased argument that the poet must have known the Egyptian river horse rather than the elephant of India or Africa.
Gill gives the verse in its own words — the beast lying in the covert of the reed.
Clarke candidly owns these habits of the behemoth are, and must be, unknown to us.

themes: the poet's supposed horizon (India versus Africa)
peaceable strength versus the lion's den

schools.summary: Gill doubts the shade fits the elephant, which rarely lies down and is reckoned taller than the trees, and inclines to the river horse of the reeds and willows.
Clarke grants that 'the willows of the brook compass him' would agree well enough with the hippopotamus — a concession from the champion of the mammoth.

themes: both witnesses inclining to the river horse

schools.summary: Gill finds 'drink up a river' too strong a hyperbole for the elephant and prefers 'let a river oppress him, he hasteth not' — the unconcerned wading of the river horse, which the elephant, fearful in water, cannot match.
Clarke reads a beast no river can stop, and from the naming of Jordan judges it once haunted the marshes of Palestine, commending Good's 'though Jordan rush against his mouth.'
Ellicott renders cleanly, 'if a river overflow, he trembleth not; he is confident, though Jordan swell up to his mouth' — magnificent composure before the flood.

debates.question: How is 'he drinketh up a river' best rendered?

sides.position: 'if a river overflow, he trembleth not' — the beast's fearless composure
'he drinketh up a river' / 'though Jordan rush against his mouth' (with Mr. Good)

schools.summary: Clarke reads the beast's contempt for restraint — his nose tearing through the stakes — closes the account with his extinct mammoth, and presses the Kennicott theory that vv.1-14 are a displaced leaf belonging after Job 42:6.
Gill reads the verse of the difficulty of capture: neither elephant nor river horse is taken openly, but decoyed by craft into a hidden pit.
Ellicott renders 'let one take him by his eyes; by snares one may pierce his nose,' judging the Authorised Version less probable.

debates.question: How is the closing clause to be read?

sides.position: 'let one take him by his eyes; by snares one may pierce his nose' — capture by stealth and allurement
'he taketh it with his eyes; his nose pierceth through snares' — the beast's contempt for restraint

outliers.note: Presses Kennicott's theory that Job 40:1-14 is a displaced leaf of the roll belonging after Job 42:6, and concludes Behemoth is an extinct mammoth preserved by providence for later ages to admire.
